item.title: Turn an ESP32 into a WiFi Motion Sensor: ESPectre Principles and Deployment
item.description: If you want to know whether someone is moving in a room, the two off-the-shelf options are both awkward. Cameras raise privacy problems and are off-limits in bedrooms and bathrooms. PIR sensors rely on infrared, fail behind a glass cabinet, and false-trigger on air-conditioning drafts. ESPectre takes a different angle: the room is already full of WiFi signals, and human movement disturbs them — so just read the change in the signal. It turns a ten-dollar ESP32 into a motion sensor with no camera, no microphone, and no dedicated mmWave radar; the router is the one you already own.

item.title: From Signals to Systems: How Platforms Build on WiFi Sensing
item.description: The previous three posts covered the physics, the detection algorithms, and two open-source projects — but between all that and “the lights come on by themselves” sits one more layer: the platform. Raw CSI and detector scores are for machines; a smart home consumes states like “bathroom occupied” or “no activity from grandma for an hour” that automations can be written against. This post takes the platform layer apart: how scores become events, events become semantics, semantics reach Home Assistant and Matter, how commercial platforms split edge and cloud, and how 802.11bf writes those roles into the protocol itself. Every mechanism comes with a living example — ESPectre and RuView on the open-source side, Cognitive Systems and ADT on the commercial side.
